feedback: Strong, near-complete capstone across all four deliverables, graded on the full readable PDFs. On D1 your catalogue carries eight of the ten findings with the right class and a quoted source line for each, which is what earns the high mark. SQLi (CWE-89, lines 64-67), unsalted MD5, alg:none (lines 48-50), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (line 30 and 38), missing exp (lines 76-81), XXE (file:///etc/passwd), open redirect and the cookie flags are all proved at the line level. Two real findings are missing from the catalogue though, the stored XSS in comments (CWE-79, the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47) and the path traversal (CWE-22, files/?path=/etc/passwd at 02:24:02), and you should add both as their own rows since they appear in your own D2 chain. Your decoy verdict is correct and honest, you named the b64url helpers and proved they make no authorization or signature decision rather than inventing an exploit, and you did not fall into the trap of calling alg:none the decoy; to reach full marks anchor the safe verdict to the mechanism, the HS256 branch is sound because it uses hash_equals which is constant-time, so the real bugs are alg:none and the hardcoded secret. D2 is excellent, the chain runs in order from recon 02:14:08 through the SQLi at 02:15:31, the 312-row export at 02:16:04, the stored XSS, the open redirect and the file read, each reconciled to a capture line with verbatim proof, and your impact paragraph states the 20-row sample, the average, the extrapolation to 312 and the BoltCash six-week window, which is exactly the reasoning we want over a bare number. The one thing to fix on D2 is the SQLi vector, you wrote A:H and 9.8 and justified it as the attacker shutting down the app, but the authentication bypass does not hit availability, so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1, and the senior insight you are missing is that a forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is a scope change to S:C. D3 is the strongest deliverable, the executive summary is jargon-free and ends on the 312-customers-and-naira headline, the threat model is complete, the decoy is restated, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by effort and risk-reduction-per-hour with real hour estimates and a why-this-rank column rather than by CVSS severity, which is the distinction most reports miss; your two stopgaps are concrete with exact Splunk fields, ModSecurity rules and false-positive justifications. Tighten D3 only by quoting the source line for the JWT findings the way you did in D1 instead of writing documented in analysis. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites Canon II and Canon I by number load-bearing, and ties the breach duty to the 312 customers, but it stops short of naming the NDPA 2023 sections, you needed section 40 for notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 for notifying data subjects on high risk, and a bare statutory window is not enough. The single most important fix is to add the two missing findings, stored XSS and path traversal, as their own catalogued rows in D1 with their quoted evidence lines, because they are already in your chain and leaving them out of the catalogue is the only real gap in an otherwise outstanding submission.
